learning_objective: 🎯 Uncover India's massive contributions to global mathematics, from the invention of zero and the decimal system to the foundations of calculus!

main_concepts.simple_explanation: India gave the world the concept of 'Zero' as both a placeholder and a standalone number. Brahmagupta was the first to formalize rules for doing arithmetic with zero and negative numbers.
The base-10 decimal system we use globally today (1, 2, 3...) was developed in India. It was later transmitted to Europe via Arab mathematicians, which is why they are called Hindu-Arabic numerals.
The Sulbasutras (rules of the chord) are ancient manuals for constructing complex fire altars (Yajnas). They contain an early statement of the Pythagorean theorem, long before Pythagoras was born!

Indian mathematicians developed modern trigonometry. Aryabhata introduced the 'Jya' (Sine) function to calculate planetary distances. The Arabic translation of 'Jya' eventually became the modern word 'Sine'.

In the 14th-16th centuries, mathematicians like Madhava in Kerala discovered infinite series and Taylor series expansions for trigonometric functions, laying the early foundations for Calculus, centuries before Newton and Leibniz.

fun_activity.title: 🧮 Multiply Like Ancient Indians
fun_activity.instructions: Search online for the 'Indian Lattice Multiplication Method' (also known as the Gelosia method). Try multiplying 45 x 23 using this cool, visual grid method. It's how complex math was done centuries ago!

exam_tips: 📌 Clearly state Brahmagupta's contribution: Formalizing the rules for Zero and negative numbers.
📌 Remember that the 'Sulbasutras' deal with Geometry (specifically for constructing fire altars).
📌 Highlight the 'Kerala School of Mathematics' when discussing the early roots of Calculus and infinite series.
quick_recap: ⭐ The place-value system and zero revolutionized calculation worldwide.
⭐ Aryabhata calculated the value of Pi (π) to 4 decimal places (3.1416).
⭐ Indian math was highly practical, developed alongside astronomy to track celestial bodies.
